content: 1. Management and Quality of Life Post-Treatment: This includes assessing their ability to manage symptoms and the overall impact of the disease and treatment on their daily lives. 2. Anti-Inflammatory Co-Administration: The use of anti-inflammatory agents in conjunction with standard TB treatment for children and adolescents with tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is highlighted as a potential therapeutic strategy. 3. Optimal Treatment Regimens for TBM in Children Living with HIV (CALHIV): Research is needed to determine the most effective treatment regimens for managing TBM in children and adolescents who are living with HIV. 4. Decentralization of TB Services: Decentralizing TB care services for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or those exposed to TB is emphasized. This approach aims to improve access to care and case detection in community settings. 5. Cost-Effectiveness of Decentralized Services: Evaluating the cost-effectiveness of decentralized and integrated TB services is critical, particularly in terms of case detection and the provision of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT). 6. Impact on Health Equity: Decentralized TB services should be assessed for their impact on health equity, ensuring that vulnerable populations have equal access to care. 7. Family-Centered and Integrated Services: These models should be evaluated for their feasibility, acceptability, and cost-effectiveness. 8. Implementation Research: Research is needed to assess the real-world implementation of family-centered and decentralized TB care programs, including their components and outcomes. 9. Outcomes of Interest: Key outcomes to monitor include the initiation of TPT, the number of additional TB cases diagnosed, delays in care, retention in treatment, treatment completion rates, clinical outcomes (e.g., treatment success), and the impact on mental health, stigma, school attendance, and equity. 10. Baseline Community Needs Assessment: Conducting community needs assessments is crucial to understand perceptions of TB care and prevention for children and adolescents, as well as to identify gaps in service delivery. 11. Improving TB Diagnosis in Children: Research should focus on enhancing the accuracy of TB diagnosis in children, addressing both under-diagnosis and over-diagnosis. 12. Use of Rapid Diagnostic Tools: Tools such as the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assays are valuable for diagnosing active TB and rifampicin resistance in children. These tools can be applied to various specimen types, including stool and gastric aspirates, to improve diagnostic accuracy. 13. Shorter Treatment Regimens: Shortened treatment regimens for non-severe TB in children have shown promise and should be further evaluated for their effectiveness and safety. 14. Drug-Resistant TB Management: The management of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) in children requires specific guidelines, including the use of newer drugs like bedaquiline and delamanid. Their safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy in pediatric populations should be closely monitored. 15. Community-Based Interventions: Expanding contact tracing and community-based case-finding strategies can significantly improve TB detection and treatment initiation among children, particularly in resource-limited settings. 16. Integration with Existing Health Systems: 17. Global and Regional Guidelines: Adherence to WHO guidelines and national TB programs is critical for standardizing care and improving outcomes for children and adolescents with TB. 18. Research and Innovation: Ongoing research and innovation are necessary to address gaps in TB care, including the development of new diagnostic tools, treatment algorithms, and preventive strategies tailored to pediatric populations. These points underscore the importance of a comprehensive, evidence-based approach to managing TB in children and adolescents, with a focus on improving access, equity, and outcomes.
